items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Clark Terry and Milt Hinton also, if he’s up to it, will be our guests with our band.

ctx.x: What’s in the immediate future? I know you’re playing tonight, which I’m looking forward to, but where do you go from here?

From here we go back to San Jose, Francine and I live in San Jose part of the time and part of the time down in Sherman Oaks, that’s near L.A. And we’re home for two days in San Jose and then we’re off to Michigan, Ypsilanti, Michigan. I’m playing with a college band there, a big jazz band, and I’m doing a piece written for me with a percussion ensemble. So I’m doing two things and then also a clinic for all the drummers. And then from there we come back home, and go down to L.A. and we get ready to go to Montana…
Oh, you gentlemen do get around, I’ll tell you.

items.title: Milt Hinton interviewed by Joe Williams, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: There was five piano players... And the drummer was Louie Bellson.

ctx.x: Oh, yeah, friends of Ellington. Yeah.
There was five piano players, you remember? Five piano players. Willie “The Lion”, Earl Hines, Marian McPartland, and Hank Jones. And the drummer was Louie Bellson. Jim Hall was the guitar player—
And Dizzy Gillespie was just in the audience. © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Milt Hinton is mentioned by the interviewer as a possible bass player in a trio, and the interviewee corrects him, stating 'No, it wasn't Milt. It was... John Heard.' ctx.x: We’ve talked about the drummers through the swing era. We talked a little bit about the New-Orleans-style drummers and the swing-era drummers. You started talking a little while back about when you first started hearing Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker. We talked about Kenny Clarke. Then earlier, off mike, we talked about Max Roach. Do you want to talk more about Max Roach?

Yeah. Max and I did the first clinic – it has to be close to 55 years ago, or maybe more. We did it in Brooklyn. Max and I were the two set players. Sol Goodwin was the tympani, and Jose Bettincourt was mallets. During that clinic, I learned so much from Max, because when I played my segment, Max told me – he says, “Lou, I got a big charge out of listening to you play. Do you ever think of the melody when you’re playing a drum solo?” I said, “No. I don’t think so.” He said, “If you are playing Cherokee, that…

with the bass players like Ray Brown and Milt Hinton and all those greats today like Christian McBride, they’ve got the four covered. So now this is syncopated – the bass drum – which you know, and the left hand is syncopated. So I learned from Dizzy. Dizzy said, “Lou” – the first time I played with him, he says, “You don’t have to play the bass drum on all four beats. You mix it up a little bit.” I found it hard to do first, because [I was] coming from that other school, but it didn’t take me long, working with…
